newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Australian voters cool quickly to PM Howard.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Australian voters cool quickly to PM Howard.

text.p: John Howard was elected Australia's first conservative leader largely because voters warmed to him as an ordinary, honest bloke.

But barely midway through his first three-year term, that asset has become a burden -- the mood of voters darkening as they turn on a prime minister that even many of his supporters now see as weak, visionless and out of his depth.

One of Australia's top social researchers, Hugh Mackay, has found voters increasingly pessimistic about the future, disillusioned with Howard's "ordinary man" style and his Liberal-National government's performance, especially its failure to tackle unemployment.

"When he came to office, he was regarded as an honest, fair and reasonable person. No one expected fireworks from him, nor did they expect he would be a big-picture visionary...," Mackay says in his annual snapshot of voter sentiment.
"But although expectations were modest, there has been significant disappointment in the prime minister's performance and, indeed, in the performance of his government," Mackay says.
FAILING POPULARITY
Howard has watched his once-commanding opinion poll lead over the Labor opposition dwindle to virtually nothing as a series of woes hit his government.
He had vowed to impose tough ethical standards on his team, but instead has been hit by a series of corruption and conflict-of-interest scandals.
The government has also been dogged by stubbornly high unemployment -- stuck above 8.5 percent -- and damaging national rows over race and Aboriginal land rights.
Howard was widely lampooned over his recent two-week visit to London, Washington and New York, which was largely portrayed as a summer holiday, fitting in some cricket in England.
Leading opinion polls support Mackay's assessment.

The government's poll lead over the Labor opposition, after hovering around 12 points for most of its first year in power, has plunged to just a few points in most surveys and is even neck-and-neck in some.
Importantly, the polls show growing dissatisfaction with the way Howard does his job. Voters unhappy with his performance heavily outweigh those who are satisfied.
EASILY INFLUENCED
Mackay found even Howard's supporters are growing increasingly disillusioned with the former suburban lawyer.

"Putting together the views of supporters and detractors, the composite picture to emerge is of a man who seems somewhat out of his depth, too easily influenced by the pressure of public opinion and too easily distracted from a clear focus," Mackay says.
One of those Mackay spoke to said: "When Little John came in, he was the most honest prime minister. Now, I think,, the job's overcome him."
Howard is respected by most Australians for showing leadership on just one big issue -- guns.

In the face of a bitter gun lobby campaign and a revolt from many in his National Party coalition partner, he forced through tough gun ownership laws in the wake of the 1996 Port Arthur massacre in which 35 people were shot dead by a lone gunman.
HIT OVER HANSON
But Howard is generally accused by the right of not going far enough on a range of economic and social issues, and by the left of going too far.
He has been widely criticised for failing to stamp out race row politician Pauline Hanson's rising popularity and influence.
His planned solution to a divisive row between Aborigines and farmers has angered everyone -- including his political allies -- and pleased no one.

Howard has put the issue of whether Australia should become a republic on the backburner, slowed the push towards free trade, adopted a softer stand on human rights issues than he signalled in opposition, and renewed Canberra's historic focus on Europe and the United States, with less enthusiasm for Asia than his Labor predecessors.

Even his efforts to rein in big government deficits have won him little support. After massive and painful spending cuts in his first budget last year, his latest effort in May was seen as merely treading water.
KEATING CONTRAST
Howard's leadership style stands out all the more for its contrast with the man he ousted, Labor's Paul Keating.

Keating -- with his penchant for French empire clocks, Italian suits and classical music -- was regarded as arrogant and out of touch. But he was respected by many for having a vision for Australia into the next century.

In his years in government, first as treasurer and later prime minister, he pushed the republican debate, lobbied hard for free trade and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and deregulated the financial system.

Despite Howard's falling public standing, and leadership jockeying between his deputy and treasurer Peter Costello and Workplace Relations Minister Peter Reith, analysts say there is no cause for alarm yet.

Although an election is expected late next year, Howard can wait until May 1999. In the meantime, his budget turnaround will at least give him a reasonable budget surplus to spend on wooing voters if he chooses.
